structured_data.engagement_pattern: Benanav's engagement with Neurath follows a consistent asymmetric gradient across all four source works. On the political-normative surface — democratic planning over market allocation, welfare pluralism over GDP maximization, planning as productive of freedom rather than antagonistic to it, the legitimacy of constructive socialist imagination — engagement is substantive and the convergence is real. On the technical-structural core — that in-kind calculation is not a transitional expedient but the permanent and necessary form of socialist economic rationality; that monetary calculation is not merely inadequate but structurally incapable of measuring social wealth; that any retention of inter-enterprise commodity exchange reproduces capitalist logic regardless of ownership form — engagement collapses into omission, framing reduction, or selective citation. The war economy argument, Neurath's primary empirical anchor for in-kind administration as historically demonstrated rather than merely theorized, is consistently reduced from normative institutional template to historical feasibility analogy. The Mises immanent critique — Neurath's most technically powerful argument — is named but not engaged. The socialist utility versus capitalist profit calculation distinction, the hinge on which the entire moneyless economy argument turns, is cited in a single footnote for its anti-reductionist conclusion while its structural implication (that no modified pricing mechanism can substitute for in-kind calculation) is ignored. The pattern is one of mining Neurath for conclusions while declining the arguments that constrain those conclusions institutionally.

key_divergences.description: Benanav correctly identifies Neurath's in-kind calculation as the key socialist response to Mises and cites it as authority for his multi-criterial framework. However, he does not reproduce Neurath's structural argument that incommensurability of welfare components is permanent and irreducible — not a transitional limitation awaiting better metrics — and that this makes in-kind calculation not a second-best solution but the only structurally adequate form of socialist economic rationality. The relief map methodology, the ordinal-but-not-cardinal welfare ranking, and the argument that plan selection requires direct political judgment rather than computation are all absent. Benanav's own multi-criterial framework depends on the incommensurability claim but derives it from a different lineage (multi-criteria optimization theory) without the philosophical justification Neurath provides, leaving it exposed to the objection that sufficiently sophisticated welfare indices could serve as common denominators. More critically, Benanav's institutional design — a dual-currency system with inter-firm market exchange and price-like signals — is precisely what Neurath argues must be structurally abolished, not supplemented or modified.
key_divergences.subtitle: In-kind calculation treated as one method among others rather than the permanent structural necessity Neurath argued
key_divergences.title: Naturalrechnung Cited Without Its Grounding Incommensurability Argument

key_divergences.description: Benanav's Beyond Capitalism 2 explicitly retains inter-firm market exchange as a permanent coordinating mechanism, justified on grounds of flexibility and adaptive responsiveness. This is precisely the institutional form Neurath identifies as the paradigm error in socialist thought — the 'capitalism of groups' thesis derived from Engels's Anti-Dühring: any scheme retaining exchange relationships among enterprises, regardless of ownership form or currency denomination, reproduces capitalist logic. Neurath's systematic argument that partial socialization without a total plan is not genuine socialization, that labour vouchers cannot regulate production even if they distribute consumption, and that market socialist prices are either arbitrary (losing their efficiency-signal function) or genuine (reproducing capitalist allocation) — all directly relevant to evaluating Benanav's proposals — are entirely absent from Benanav's engagement. The silence is structural: engaging this argument would require Benanav either to defend his market-exchange mechanism against it or to concede that his proposals fall outside Neurath's definition of genuine socialism.
key_divergences.subtitle: Beyond Capitalism retains inter-firm commodity exchange while invoking Neurathian authority for planning
key_divergences.title: Neurath's Anti-Market-Socialist Argument Absent Despite Direct Relevance

key_divergences.description: Benanav cites Neurath's 1925 'Socialist Utility Calculation and Capitalist Profit Calculation' in a footnote as authority for the non-substitutability of values. This is the favorable slice of Neurath's position. But the same text contains the argument that socialist calculation and capitalist profit calculation are structurally incompatible forms of economic rationality — not merely differently oriented, but requiring qualitatively different institutional forms — because the socialist goal (maximum quality of life for all) is formally incommensurable while the capitalist goal (maximum monetary gain per enterprise) defines a single commensurable objective for which unit calculation is appropriate. The implication that no modification of the pricing mechanism, including dual currencies, can substitute for in-kind calculation in a genuinely socialist economy is precisely what Benanav needs to confront and does not. The citation provides Neurathian authority for the conclusion while the argument that constrains its institutional implications is omitted.
key_divergences.subtitle: The normative foundation of Neurath's economic program invoked for conclusions while its structural implications are ignored
key_divergences.title: Socialist Utility vs. Capitalist Profit Distinction Cited Without Its Technical Core

key_divergences.description: Neurath's war-economy argument is specifically an institutional transition argument: the organizational apparatus created by wartime necessity — central offices, in-kind rationing, bulk reserves, suspension of profit as allocative signal — constitutes the embryo of socialist administration and can be directly occupied and extended. Benanav consistently reduces this to a generic feasibility demonstration: large-scale non-market coordination is historically possible. The specific institutional argument — that socialization in 1919 required 'only a small additional political step' precisely because the organizational apparatus already existed — is never engaged. This reduction strips Neurath's most distinctive empirical claim of its operational content, and leaves Benanav's own institutional proposals (Investment Boards, Data Matrix, Technical Associations) without the empirical-transitional anchor Neurath provides, making them more abstract and less actionable relative to the Neurathian benchmark they invoke.
key_divergences.subtitle: The empirical anchor of Neurath's planning theory stripped of its transitional and organizational content
key_divergences.title: War Economy Reduced from Institutional Template to Historical Analogy

key_divergences.description: Benanav's core welfare argument — that benefits across different criteria cannot be reduced to a single metric and that plan selection requires direct political judgment rather than technical optimization — replicates Neurath's conditions-of-life framework and relief map methodology. The credit given to Neurath focuses on his institutional proposals rather than the welfare epistemology that is more directly operative in Benanav's own argument. By not acknowledging the debt at the philosophical level, Benanav misses the opportunity to deploy Neurath's most sophisticated arguments against the objection that multi-criterial frameworks merely reflect normative preferences rather than structural features of rational social choice. The unacknowledged debt also means the framework inherits the conclusion without the argument, leaving the incommensurability claim underdefended.
key_divergences.subtitle: Conditions-of-life framework and relief map methodology operative in Benanav's argument but unacknowledged at the philosophical level
key_divergences.title: Multi-Criterial Welfare Framework Derived from Neurath Without Full Acknowledgment

key_divergences.description: Benanav presents Neurath's central office for calculation in kind as a precedent for democratic deliberation over alternative plans — accurate as far as it goes. But in Neurath's argument, the central office functions as the institutional replacement for market price signals throughout the economy, including at the enterprise level: the efficiency of individual firms can only be assessed by their fit within a better total plan, not by their own operational balance. Benanav's firms retain operational autonomy and face market-like budget constraints (the points system) that allow enterprise-level efficiency assessment without reference to a total in-kind plan. By invoking Neurath's institutional proposal while stripping it from the context that makes it intelligible — its anti-price-signal function at the micro level — Benanav creates the impression of Neurathian institutional grounding for an architecture Neurath would classify as partial socialization.
key_divergences.subtitle: Neurath's central institutional proposal decontextualized from the micro-level replacement function that makes it structurally significant
key_divergences.title: The Economic Plan Invoked Without Its Anti-Price-Signal Function at the Firm Level

structured_data.reading_implications: Readers of Benanav's Beyond Capitalism essays should approach the Neurathian framework with a calibrated skepticism about what has and has not been inherited. The genuine intellectual debts are real and consequential: Benanav correctly identifies Neurath's multi-criterial orientation, his democratic utopianism, and his argument that planning can produce rather than constrain freedom as important resources for contemporary socialist thought. These inheritances are not merely rhetorical — they structure the substantive architecture of Benanav's proposals. However, the specific institutional conclusions Benanav draws — that a dual-currency market system retaining inter-firm commodity exchange and price-like signals can constitute a genuine post-capitalist economy — are precisely what Neurath's technical arguments are designed to rule out. Readers who encounter Neurath in Benanav's footnotes and treat the citation as evidence that Benanav's institutional design is Neurathian in its foundations should read Neurath's 'Economic Plan and Calculation in Kind' and 'Socialist Utility Calculation and Capitalist Profit Calculation' directly. Those texts contain the arguments Benanav does not engage: that in-kind calculation is the permanent structural form of socialist rationality (not a transitional expedient), that the socialist utility versus capitalist profit distinction entails specific institutional requirements no pricing mechanism can substitute for, and that any economy retaining enterprise-level commodity exchange — however modified its currency form — falls on the wrong side of the line between genuine socialism and what Neurath calls 'capitalism of groups.' The implication is that Benanav's post-scarcity and automation arguments, evaluated against the Neurath he invokes as authority, occupy a theoretical position closer to sophisticated market socialism than to Neurath's moneyless administrative economy — a position Neurath spent considerable energy arguing against. Whether Benanav's framework is nonetheless defensible on its own terms is a separate question; the AOI finding is that it cannot straightforwardly claim Neurathian warrant for its institutional design while remaining silent on Neurath's central institutional argument.

sin_distribution.description: Benanav cites Neurath's in-kind calculation proposal and his socialist utility vs. capitalist profit distinction as authority for the multi-criterial framework while engaging only their anti-reductionist conclusions. The philosophical arguments that ground those conclusions — permanent incommensurability, the structural difference between socialist and capitalist calculation regimes — are not reproduced, leaving the framework without the strongest available defense of its foundational claims.

Two critical omissions with structural significance: Neurath's immanent critique of Mises (showing that even Mises concedes a non-monetary welfare standard, thereby undermining the case for monetary calculation as uniquely rational) is named but not engaged, despite its direct relevance to Benanav's defense of non-monetary planning. Neurath's systematic argument against market socialism and labour-money (any retention of enterprise-level commodity exchange reproduces capitalist logic) is entirely absent, despite being directly applicable to Benanav's dual-currency market mechanism.

The war economy argument is consistently reduced from a normative institutional model — whose specific organizational forms (central offices, in-kind rationing, suspension of profit) provide the direct empirical template for socialist transition — to a generic historical analogy demonstrating political feasibility. This strips the argument of its most distinctive content: the claim that the transition to socialism runs through already-existing institutional forms.

Benanav's multi-criterial welfare framework — built around the non-compensatory, ordinally rankable but not cardinally measurable character of welfare components — directly replicates Neurath's conditions-of-life framework and relief map methodology. The credit given to Neurath focuses on his institutional proposals rather than the welfare epistemology operative in Benanav's own argument, constituting an unacknowledged philosophical debt.

Neurath's central office for calculation in kind is invoked as precedent for democratic deliberation while being stripped from the context that gives it structural significance: its function as the institutional replacement for price signals at the enterprise level, not merely a macro-level investment coordination mechanism.

Benanav invokes Neurath's social engineering methodology — multiple alternative plans, democratic submission, anti-propagandist utopianism — to legitimize his constructive planning vision, while proposing institutional mechanisms (dual-currency market exchange, firm-level operational autonomy with price-like signals) that Neurath regards as precluding the transparency that makes social engineering meaningful. Neurath's methodological authority is deployed for an institutional program he would not endorse.

structured_data.summary: Benanav's two-part Beyond Capitalism essay engages Neurath substantively but asymmetrically. The engagement is genuine and consequential where Neurath functions as a methodological and political resource — scientific utopianism, democratic planning, the incompatibility of single-criterion optimization with socialist aims, and the compatibility of planning with freedom. It becomes selective, distorting, or strategically silent precisely where Neurath is most technically distinctive: the permanent structural necessity of in-kind calculation, the categorical rejection of any economy retaining commodity exchange among enterprises, and the specific institutional architecture (central measurement office, multidimensional in-kind plan, universal statistics) that gives those conclusions their operational force. The net result is that Benanav invokes Neurathian authority for a post-capitalist planning project whose institutional core — a dual-currency market system retaining inter-firm exchange and price-like signals — is precisely the hybrid form Neurath argued, at length, was structurally incapable of constituting genuine socialism. Whether this constitutes productive creative misreading, selective appropriation, or inadvertent legitimation borrowing is the central question the evidence forces, and on balance the answer is selective appropriation shading into legitimation borrowing: Benanav takes Neurath's conclusions without Neurath's arguments, and deploys Neurath's authority for institutional arrangements Neurath explicitly argued against.
